newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Suharto son denies family ties boost business.
newsitem.headline: Suharto son denies family ties boost business.

text.p: Indonesian President Suharto's youngest son on Thursday denied persistent criticism his business empire was based on family links and said recent street riots did not reflect a popular push for more freedom.

"I am part of the family, but the important thing is the (business) activity itself, how we convince the government to implement these ideas," Hutomo "Tommy" Mandala Putra told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio in a rare interview from Jakarta.
"We are having equal treatment to other businessmen or business activity in Indonesia. We fairly often lose our... (bids)."
Mandala Putra, whose diversified business interests include car production, cloves and aviation, is ranked as one of his country's richest ethnic Indonesians.
The extensive business operations of Suharto's six children have come in for domestic and foreign criticism on the grounds they have been favoured in government contracts and licences.
Mandala Putra said recent street protests in the capital were common in countries with rapid economic growth and did not reflect a popular push for more freedom.

"Regarding the 27th of July (riots), I think it's happening in any country, even in Korea, (which is) having very successful economic growth, they still have a problem with their university students," he said.
"So they cannot say that they are (acting) on behalf of the people of Indonesia, or they call it people power... I mean it's nothing."
Riots broke out in central Jakarta in July after police took over the national headquarters of the Indonesian Democratic Party to install a government-backed faction.
Mandala Putra said his father had brought stability to Indonesia in his three decades at the helm of the world's fourth most populous nation.
"(Indonesia is) very stable, I think not only at the moment but in the past 30 years since my father took over the country, I think national stability is there," he said.
He defended Indonesia's openness and rejected calls for more freedom and increased democracy. "We are free, we can do anything in this country," Mandala Putra said.

"Of course, you have to follow the regulations, not only here, even in the (United) States, which has the most freedom they say. You can do anything here, except you cannot disturb other people's activity."
